Amy Zhang: Heads-up — quick sync on dedicated-pool autoscaling policy and SLA fallbacks. TL;DR: we need clearer ownership boundaries between headroom budgeting and latency SLOs when bursts hit. cc @Ben @Chao
Ben Ortiz: +1. Can you sketch the problem scenario briefly?
Amy Zhang: Example: tenant A normally uses reserved capacity. Sudden traffic spike consumes headroom, autoscaler takes 40s to add GPUs, operator falls back to a cheaper dedicated-burst lane which routes to a different model variant. P99 latency jumps and customer sees errors. We need an explicit policy and clear operator<>controller contract.
Chao Li: I keep thinking admission vs execution split. Admit should be a fast, deterministic call that either grants a short-lived prewarm token or rejects. Execution uses the token to route. That avoids racing on allocation.
Rachel Park: Telemetry ask: we need per-tenant headroom burn-rate, prewarm token issuances, and evictions emitted as events so SLO/alerting can separate admission noise from actual infra failures.
Jorge Mendes: Proposed fallback hierarchy (rough): 1) tenant dedicated pool 2) tenant burst lane (soft reserved) 3) regional dedicated shard 4) hosted fallback (with opt-in). Each step annotated with an SLO tag and cost multiplier.
Amy Zhang: here's a tiny config sketch to make ideas concrete:
```yaml
autoscaling:
  headroom_percent: 8
  burst_policy: soft_reserve
  prewarm_ttl_secs: 45
  fallback_order: [tenant_burst, regional_dedicated, hosted_api]
```
Ben Ortiz: + config looks good. We should keep prewarm_ttl small to reduce wasted resource holding. But be careful: too small -> fails to catch slow scale-ups.
Chao Li: Agree. Also: Admit -> returns { token_id, lease_ttl, warmup_hint }. Example pseudocode:
```go
func Admit(req) (Token, error) {
  // idempotent by client-provided request_id
}
```
Tokens should be lightweight and short lived. Make Admit idempotent to reduce double-grant races.
Rachel Park: On metrics, propose these new counters/gauges: dedicated.headroom_available, dedicated.headroom_burn_rate, prewarm.tokens_issued, prewarm.tokens_failed, fallback.invoked_by_tier. Dashboards + alerting thresholds for headroom depletion.
Jorge Mendes: For fallback cost accounting: track tenant->fallback mapping and chargebacks so finance sees when hosted fallbacks spike costs. Also add a circuit-breaker: if fallback cost in window > X, stop fallback and degrade gracefully (throttle).
Amy Zhang: Rollout plan ideas: canary on a single shard (5% tenants) with telemetry gating: P99 latency, error-rate, and fallback-rate. If any exceed thresholds, rollback.
Ben Ortiz: Small experiment: flip the admit idempotency + token ttl on a single shard and run synthetic traffic shaped like tenant bursts. I'll own the canary.
Chao Li: Race note: operator may see token and start prewarm then node gets preempted. Need eviction_risk signal from operator to controller so controller can top up headroom or re-issue tokens.
Rachel Park: Also we need logs for token lifecycle to make post-incident tracing easier: ISSUE -> token_issued -> prewarm_started -> prewarm_completed -> token_consumed/expired/evicted.
Jorge Mendes: I'll draft an RFC with: problem statement, fallback taxonomy, Admit API surface, token lifecycle, metrics, rollout checklist, and cost guardrails. Expect a first draft tomorrow.
